title: Lifetimes
intro: A lifetime is the stretch of the program during which a reference is valid. Every reference has one, and the compiler usually works it out. You write one, like `'a`, when a signature or a struct has to say which values a reference borrows from. It describes a link the compiler checks. It never makes anything live longer.

coming_from.go: Go has no lifetimes: the garbage collector keeps whatever you can still reach alive. Rust has no collector, so a function that returns a reference, or a struct that stores one, names the input it borrows from with `'a`, and the compiler checks the link.
coming_from.kotlin: The JVM keeps an object alive while any reference to it exists, so there is nothing to annotate. In Rust `'a` is a label saying which inputs a returned or stored reference borrows from. The compiler checks the label; it does not change how long anything lives.
coming_from.python: Python keeps an object alive while a name or container still refers to it, so nothing needs naming. In Rust, `'a` is a label for "this reference borrows from that input", and the compiler rejects any use of it after the input is gone.
coming_from.typescript: JavaScript's garbage collector keeps an object alive while it is reachable, and TypeScript's types never mention it. In Rust a signature or struct that holds a reference says which value it borrows from (`'a`), and the compiler checks every use.
coming_from.java: Java keeps an object alive while any reference to it exists, so no signature says how long a result is valid. In Rust `'a` says it: the result borrows from these inputs and is valid while they are.
coming_from.csharp: The .NET garbage collector keeps an object alive while it is reachable. The nearest compile-time ideas are `Span<T>`, which the compiler stops from escaping, and the `scoped` keyword; Rust applies a check of this kind to every reference and names the link with `'a`.
coming_from.c: A C pointer carries no lifetime, so which input a returned pointer points into, and until when, lives in a comment. Rust writes it in the signature (`'a`) and checks every use.
coming_from.cpp: A C++ reference or `std::string_view` carries no lifetime in its type either. Compilers flag a few recognised shapes, and clang has an opt-in `[[clang::lifetimebound]]` attribute, but nothing checks every call. `'a` is the same contract, written in the signature and checked everywhere.

notes: `'a` is a name. `longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str` says: the result borrows from `a` and from `b`, so it is valid only while both are. The signature describes the link; the compiler checks it. Writing `'a` never keeps a value alive.

Most signatures need none. When the inputs have exactly one lifetime, or the method has `&self`, the compiler fills in the obvious link (the elision rules). You write `'a` when two or more inputs could be the source, or when a struct holds a reference.

`struct Excerpt<'a> { part: &'a str }` says an `Excerpt` cannot outlive the text its `part` points into. A struct that owns its data (`String`, `Vec`) has no lifetime to write, which is why the Structs lesson had none.

`'static` is the longest lifetime: string literals have it, and `T: 'static` means "`T` holds no borrow that ends early". Code that owns its data (`String`, `Vec`) writes few lifetimes, and when they start to pile up, owning the data is usually the way out.

gotcha.title: A result used after one of its inputs is gone
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, Java, Kotlin, Python, TypeScript and C#, `result` refers to one of the two strings and that string stays valid for as long as `result` refers to it. Here the result is `s1`, which is still in scope, so nothing can go wrong. (C and C++ are the exceptions; see their entries.)
gotcha.rust_sees: The signature says the result may borrow from `a` or from `b`; which one depends on the lengths at run time. The compiler checks the call with the signature alone, so it must assume the result could be `s2`, which is dropped at the closing `}` while `result` is still used.
gotcha.why: This run would be fine, because `s1` is the longer string. The compiler reasons from types, not from values, and with a shorter `s1` the same code would read freed memory, so it refuses both. The six garbage-collected languages never break on this shape, because the collector keeps `s2`'s string alive for as long as `result` refers to it. In C and C++ the shorter-`s1` version is a real use after free. Adding more `'a` annotations cannot help: they only describe the link, they do not lengthen it. Keep `s2` in scope as long as `result` is used, as `fixed.rs` does, or return an owned `String`.

go.says: Go runs this and prints both lines. The strings are built at run time, so they are garbage-collected values, not literals. `s2` and `s3` are only names that went out of scope: the second line shows that `result` keeps the longer string alive after the block ends.

With a shorter `s1` and a longer `s2`, `result` points into an array that is out of scope after the block, and AddressSanitizer reports stack-use-after-scope (the C and C++ block below shows the run).

cpp.says: C++ runs this and prints the long string here, because the result is `s1`. The signature returns a reference but does not say into which argument. With a shorter `s1` and a longer `s2`, `result` points at a destroyed `std::string`, and AddressSanitizer reports heap-use-after-free (the C and C++ block below shows the run).

python.code:
# Nothing to annotate: an object stays alive while anything refers to it.
def longest(a, b):
    return a if len(a) >= len(b) else b


class Excerpt:
    def __init__(self, part):
        self.part = part


novel = "Call me Ishmael. Some years ago..."
first = novel.split(".")[0]
excerpt = Excerpt(first)
l = longest(excerpt.part, "short")
print("longest:", l)
print("excerpt length:", len(excerpt.part))

class Parser:
    def __init__(self, text):
        self.rest = text

    def next_word(self):
        trimmed = self.rest.lstrip()
        if not trimmed:
            return None
        word, _, self.rest = trimmed.partition(" ")
        return word


parser = Parser("lifetimes are regions")
a = parser.next_word()
b = parser.next_word()  # a is still usable: no annotation needed
print("a:", a)
print("b:", b)
again = Parser("lifetimes are regions").next_word()
print("same object as a:", a is again)
